extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP policymakers, government officials, and researchers studying exceptions and limitations to patent rights in Argentina
extracted.subtask_description: Country-specific summary of statutory standards, exceptions, limitations and procedures under Argentine patent law (Law No. 24.481 and related regulations and laws) relevant to determining patentability, exclusive rights, and permissible uses without authorization (e.g., experimental use, exhaustion, compulsory licensing, government use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is patentable if it is covered by the definition of “invention” contained in the Law on Patents, is new, has inventive step and is capable of industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source: Law No. 24.481 (consolidated text, 1996) and Regulations. The product or process must not fall within statutory exclusions. The application must contain a description sufficiently clear and complete to allow a person with average skill in the art to carry it out, including the best method known, elements set out clearly and precisely, and methods/procedures directly applicable to production. See National Patent Administration Guidelines for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application disclosure requirements (sufficiency/best mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must contain a description of the invention that is sufficiently clear and complete to allow a person with average skill in the art to carry it out, and must contain the best method known of carrying out and putting into practice the invention, with elements used set out in a clear and precise manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods and procedures described must be directly applicable to production. This requirement is part of the patentability standard under Law No. 24.481 and its Regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exclusions from patentability (Article 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following shall not be considered to be inventions: (a) discoveries, scientific theories, and mathematical methods; (b) literary or artistic works or any aesthetic creation, as well as scientific works; (c) plans, rules and methods for the practice of intellectual activity, for games or economic-commercial activities, as well as computer programs; (d) the manner of presenting information; (e) methods of surgical, therapeutic or diagnostic treatment applicable to the human body and to animals; (f) the juxtaposition of known inventions or mixtures of known products, or alteration of the form, dimensions or materials thereof, except where in reality they are so combined or merged that they cannot function separately or where their particular qualities or functions have been modified so as to produce an industrial result not obvious to a person skilled in the art; (g) all living material and substances preexisting in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation further states: “Plants, animals and the essentially biological processes for their reproduction shall not be considered to be patentable material.” Source: Article 6, Law No. 24.481 and corresponding regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional unpatentable subject-matter (Article 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) inventions whose exploitation should be prevented to protect public order or morality, the health or life of persons or animals, or to ensure conservation of plants or avoid serious environmental damage; (b) biological and genetic material occurring in nature or derived therefrom by reproduction, and genetic reproduction processes replicating nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation: the National Executive may prohibit manufacture and commercialization where necessary to protect public order/morality, human/animal/plant life or health, or avoid serious prejudice to the environment. Source: Article 7 and its regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive rights conferred by a patent (Article 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent confers on its owner exclusive rights: (a) for a product patent, to prevent third parties from making, using, offering for sale, selling, or importing the product without consent; (b) for a process patent, to prevent third parties from using the process and using, offering for sale, selling, or importing for these purposes the product obtained directly by that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source: Article 8, Law No. 24.481. Note: publication of a patent application does not accord exclusive rights to the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of patent application does not confer rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of a patent application does not accord exclusive rights to the patent applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit statement in the questionnaire response referencing Argentine law practice (Article 8 context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated exceptions and limitations categories
rubrics_metrics.description: List of statutory exceptions/limitations present in Argentine law: Private and/or non‑commercial use; Prior use; Experimental use and/or scientific research; Preparation of medicines; Use of articles on foreign vessels, aircrafts and land vehicles; Acts for obtaining regulatory approval from authorities; Exhaustion of patent rights; Compulsory licensing and/or government use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the set of topics covered in the statute(s) and questionnaire (Article 36 and other provisions). Each category is addressed in detail elsewhere in the law and regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private/academic non-commercial experimental/testing/teaching exception (Article 36(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The right conferred by a patent shall not have any effect against a third party who, in the private or academic sphere and for non-commercial purposes, engages in scientific or technological research activities for purely experimental, testing or teaching purposes, and to that end manufactures or uses a product or a process identical to the one patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 36(a), Law No. 24.481. Law does not define 'non-commercial' or 'experimental use' in the statute; the questionnaire notes no further statutory criteria or judicial clarifications were provided in the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of medicines exception (Article 36(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The right conferred by a patent shall not have any effect against the preparation of medicines by an authorized professional person and by unit following a medical prescription, or acts relating to medicines so prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 36(b), Law No. 24.481. The law indicates the exception exists and that it applies to authorized professionals preparing medicines unit-by-unit following a prescription. The law affirms there are limitations on the amount of medicines that can be prepared, but the questionnaire response does not specify the quantitative limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use / transition-period use (Article 101 and regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions protect third parties who were exploiting an invention before certain dates: the patent owner shall have exclusive rights five years after the publication of the law unless third parties making use without authorization can guarantee full supply of the domestic market at the same current prices, in which case the patent owner is entitled only to fair and reasonable remuneration from the date of grant to expiry. Regulation specifies initiation of acts of exploitation or significant investment prior to January 1, 1995 is required to limit remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source: Article 101, Law No. 24.481 and corresponding regulation. In absence of agreement, the National Industrial Property Institute (INPI) sets remuneration per Article 43. These provisions reflect transitional arrangements and conditions under which prior users may continue exploitation subject to remuneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use — remuneration to patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Where prior users continue exploiting an invention, the patent owner shall have the right to receive a fair and reasonable reward from the third parties making use of the patent from the date of its grant to its expiry; in the absence of agreement the NATIONAL INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY INSTITUTE shall set said reward under Article 43.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 101 (and cross-reference to Article 43) provides the statutory basis for remuneration and INPI's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use on foreign vessels, aircraft and land vehicles (Article 36(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of inventions patented in Argentina on foreign land vehicles, vessels or aircraft accidentally or temporarily travelling in the jurisdiction of the Republic of Argentina, if they are used exclusively for the needs of said vehicles, is not affected by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 36(d), Law No. 24.481. The statute uses the terms 'accidentally' or 'temporarily' and conditions the exception on exclusive use for the needs of such vehicles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approval (Bolar-type) exception (Law 24.766, Art. 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any third party may use the invention prior to the expiry of the patent, for experimental purposes and in order to collect the information required for approval for marketing of a product or procedure by the competent authority after the expiry of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source: Article 8, Law 24.766. Applied broadly to regulatory approval of all products; statute specifies permitted acts are for experimental purposes to collect required approval data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of patent rights — international exhaustion (Article 36(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The right conferred by a patent shall not have any effect against anyone acquiring, using, importing or in any way marketing the patented product or the product obtained by means of the patented process, after said product has been lawfully placed on the market in any country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 36(c), Law No. 24.481. Regulation clarifies marketing is lawful if in accordance with TRIPS Part III, Section 4, and provides criteria for when a product is deemed lawfully placed on the market (e.g., authorization proofs by owner/licensed party). The questionnaire indicates Argentina follows international exhaustion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licensing framework (Articles 42–50)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision is made for compulsory licenses under Articles 42 to 50 titled 'Other uses without the authorization of the patent owner'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions set out procedural and substantive rules for granting compulsory licenses and government-ordered exploitation; see subsequent metric entries for grounds and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for compulsory licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds listed include non-working or insufficient working of the patented invention; refusal to grant licenses on reasonable terms; anti‑competitive practices and/or unfair competition; public health; national security; national emergency and/or extreme urgency; dependent patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These grounds are enumerated in the questionnaire response summarizing Law No. 24.481 (Articles 42–50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑working / insufficient working definition and time thresholds (Article 43)
rubrics_metrics.description: If three years have elapsed following a patent grant, or four years following the filing of the application, except in case of force majeure, and the invention has not been exploited or effective preparations have not been made, or exploitation interrupted for more than one year, any person may apply for authorization to use the invention without authorization of its owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 43 defines force majeure to include objective technical/legal difficulties such as delays in obtaining marketing approval; lack of financial resources or feasibility alone does not justify. Regulation: exploitation considered to take place if distribution/marketing are sufficient to satisfy domestic market demands under reasonable commercial conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time period before requesting compulsory license (non-working) — 3/4 years
rubrics_metrics.description: A compulsory license on grounds of non‑working or insufficient working may be requested after THREE (3) years from patent grant or FOUR (4) years from filing, except in cases of force majeure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 43 sets the statutory waiting periods and exceptions for force majeure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to license — reasonable terms and 150‑day negotiation period (Article 42)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a proposed user has made efforts to obtain a license from the owner under reasonable commercial terms and conditions and such efforts have not been successful following a period of ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY (150) consecutive days from the date on which the license was requested, the National Industrial Property Institute may allow other uses without authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 42 requires attempts to negotiate on reasonable terms for 150 days before administrative authorization; there is also an obligation to notify competition authorities (Law No. 22.262 or its successor) for relevant purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑competitive practices as ground for compulsory license (Article 44)
rubrics_metrics.description: The competent authority may grant compulsory licenses if the patent owner engaged in anti‑competitive practices. Examples deemed anti‑competitive include: (a) fixing excessive or discriminatory prices relative to average market prices; (b) refusal to supply the local market under reasonable commercial conditions; (c) obstruction of commercial or production activities; (d) any other act punishable under competition law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 44 lists these examples and allows bypassing the usual Article 42 procedure where anti‑competitive practices are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent patents — conditions for compulsory license (Article 46)
rubrics_metrics.description: A compulsory license to exploit a second patent that cannot be exploited without infringing a first patent shall be granted provided: (a) the second patent involves an important technical advance of considerable economic significance over the first; (b) the owner of the first patent is entitled to obtain a cross‑license on reasonable terms to use the second invention; (c) the authorized use in respect of the first patent shall be non‑assignable except with assignment of the second patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 46 sets cumulative substantive conditions that must all be met for dependent‑patent compulsory licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration policy for compulsory licenses (Articles 47(h) and 48)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where uses are permitted without authorization, the rightholder shall be paid reasonable remuneration considering the economic value of the authorization; remuneration determination follows Article 43 procedure. Decisions on uses not authorized are subject to judicial review, including remuneration issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 47(h) and Article 48: in cases of anti‑competitive practices, the need to correct such practices must be considered and termination of authorization may be refused if conditions leading to the license are likely to recur.

rubrics_metrics.name: National emergency / government use (Article 45)
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Executive may, for purposes of health emergency or national security, order the exploitation of certain patents (government use); the scope and duration of exploitation shall be limited to the purpose of the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 45; regulation requires involvement of relevant ministries (Economy, INPI, Health, Defense) within their competences. This is distinct from administrative compulsory licenses and applies in emergencies or for national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to establish limited exceptions (Article 41)
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Industrial Property Institute, following a reasoned request from a competent authority, may establish exceptions limited to the rights conferred by a patent provided such exceptions do not unreasonably conflict with the normal exploitation of the patent or unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the patent owner, taking into account legitimate interests of third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 41 establishes an administrative mechanism for tailored, limited exceptions upon request from competent authorities (Ministry of Economy, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Defense as appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Farmers’ and breeders’ protections and interplay with plant variety law
rubrics_metrics.description: Argentina acceded to the 1978 UPOV Act via Law 24.376 (which does not permit cumulative protection). Plant varieties are protected through Law No. 20.247 on Seeds and Phytogenetic Creations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questionnaire notes consequent treatment of breeders’/farmers’ exceptions follows those instruments; no further statutory exceptions for farmers in the patent law response were provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaps or unspecified items flagged in official responses
rubrics_metrics.description: For several questions the response indicates '[Note from the Secretariat: response was not provided]' meaning the official reply did not supply definitions or examples for terms such as 'non‑commercial', 'experimental use', public policy objectives, or detailed case law on some points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should note those lacunae where the questionnaire response left items unanswered; supplementary research (case law, administrative practice, INPI guidelines) may be needed to flesh out practical application.
